units: workers put up a metal structure in front of the building next door
the din of the assembly disturbs the flats on the floor
a sheet stretched over the front wall takes the tenants' view away
the caretaker warns the residents that the call system will be cut off
three households voice their displeasure
a temporary stand-in device is adopted
contact between neighbors becomes more frequent
the longest-standing resident finds the situation unheard of
text: Dear neighbor, here is an account of the week, exactly as I observed it unfolding from my window. It began with workmen bolting a steel framework together outside the neighboring building, and the clanging metalwork awakened everybody on our floor. Then a green tarp went up over the front wall, eliminating our view of the courtyard. Next morning the caretaker went door to door: the entry buzzer would be off while the lobby is redone. Three households complained loudly, and something came of it, a spare bell screwed onto a plank, standing in for the real one. By the end of the week the work had quietly rearranged us. We run into each other on the sidewalk, our conversations last longer nowadays, and the woman who has lived on our staircase longest swears she has seen nothing like it since she moved in. Love,

units: neither the designer nor the residents decide on their own what a district looks like
the shape of a district comes out of a long argument between opposing sides
a piece of abandoned ground usually sets off that argument
the emptiness of the place draws proposals for what to build there
the proposals bring shared memories back up
what one side asks for cannot be squared with what the other asks
the local body has to choose between those demands
the public clash usually deepens the bond to the place
text: Who decides what a neighborhood looks like? Not the designer alone, and not the people living there alone either. The answer comes out of a slow argument that sets them against one another as much as it brings them together. What sets that argument off? A patch of abandoned ground, most of the time, fenced in, thick with nettles, claimed by nobody. Because the emptiness unsettles people, it attracts plans, and because it attracts plans, it wakes up what everyone remembers. And then? One side wants vegetable beds, another wants a room for music, and the council has to rule on wishes that cannot be squared with each other. Does the quarrel damage the street? Rarely, say those who have been through one. Contradicting each other in public is how people come to know their neighbors, and the place ends up mattering more.

units: a maintenance worker lays out a fault before a meeting of occupants
water getting in eats away at the connections of the outdoor box
every spell of rain cuts the link
an occupant asks whether the whole thing has to be replaced
the worker reckons a cover, fresh sealing and new ducting will do
the woman in charge of the accounts asks what the work will cost
the sum he gives is below the price of a complete unit
an occupant from the top of the building reports a crackle in her handset
text: The maintenance man stood up and laid the fault out for the committee of residents. Water has been getting into the entry panel, he said, and it eats the contacts, so any rainfall kills the line immediately. A resident asked whether complete replacement was necessary. No, he answered: a stainless cover, fresh sealing, and replacement ducting run up from the basement would keep the circuit dry. The woman who keeps the accounts wanted to know what that would cost. He gave a modest sum, well under the price of a complete door unit, provided the way into the service room is cleared for him. A tenant from the top floor mentioned that her handset had been crackling since the fall. He wrote the remark down and offered to look at her cable that same afternoon, before he closed the box up again.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: older communities were organized differently depending on where they settled
some grew up beside a spring, others where two trading roads crossed
beside the water, authority served to share out a scarce resource
households there were counted and the turns of use written down
cheating there cost a person standing among the rest
at the crossing, the assembly saw above all to making trade safe
it set the measures and settled disputes
shared memory still differs according to those two beginnings
the institutions we have keep the mark of both patterns
text: Older communities did not arrange their common life the same way, and where they had settled accounts for much of the difference. Some grew up beside a spring, others where two trading roads crossed. Beside the water, authority came down to sharing out what there was too little of. Households were counted, turns at the channels were written down, and whoever took more than his share sank in the regard of the rest. At the crossing, wealth came with the traffic, so the assembly cared less about dividing than about keeping exchange safe. It fixed the weights, ruled on disputes, punished cheating. The two patterns left different memories behind. Where water gave the orders, people recall dry years and feuds; where trade did, they recall fairs, ruin, and the alliances that followed. Our institutions still carry both marks.

units: a neighborhood group rests on supports anyone can name
its members begin by listing what is needed and who can give what
a place to meet is needed if anything is to get done
meetings on a fixed date are worth more than enthusiasm that comes and goes
bringing in new participants keeps the active core from burning out
clear accounts keep mistrust away
newcomers must be taken in without an unspoken pecking order
a group missing one of these supports goes on, but attracts no newcomers
text: A neighborhood group stands on supports anyone can name. The first is the survey. Before acting, the members write down what is lacking around them and what the people nearby can offer: ages, languages spoken, trades, spare hours. The second is a room. With nowhere to sit down together, good intentions evaporate. The third is rhythm, because a meeting held on a fixed date is worth more than a burst of eagerness that comes and goes. The fourth is fresh hands: when the same few carry everything, they wear thin and the group dies out. The fifth is open accounts, since anything kept dark breeds suspicion. The last support is the hardest to see, which is taking newcomers in without laying an unspoken pecking order on them. A group that lets one of these go still goes on, but it attracts no newcomers.

units: a musical instrument is taken out through an opening high up in a building
it hangs from a brightly colored strap
at first there are very few onlookers
a crowd of the curious ends up filling the roadway
the workman moving it does not answer the comments
he braces the load against the frame set up for redoing the front wall
a resident fears for her vehicle parked underneath
the arrival on the ground sets off applause
the owner offers a drink to those who watched
she has loathed the object since her marriage
text: You will not believe it: a piano emerged from a third-floor window on an orange strap. Initially maybe three of us stood watching, heads tipped back. Then somebody stopped, then somebody else, and before long a crowd was filling the roadway, calling out judgments on the operation as though it were street theater. The mover said nothing back. He hauled on his rope, braced the case against the frame put up for redoing the front wall, let it down a notch, began again. A woman upstairs kept fretting over her car, parked right underneath. When the thing touched the ground the crowd clapped, which finally got a grin out of him. The best came later. The owner, a very dignified lady, asked the whole sidewalk in for a drink, to mark the going of an object she had loathed since her marriage.

units: clearing a piece of neglected ground calls for planning beforehand
the owner's permission is what makes the work lawful
without that permission nothing that gets damaged is covered
probing the soil prevents injuries from buried waste
the jobs must be handed out before the participants show up
with no jobs handed out, part of the group stands around waiting
thick gloves and plenty of containers are needed
a heap left behind draws further dumping
food shared at the end brings the participants back
text: Clearing a piece of neglected ground calls for a method worked out beforehand, or the volunteers drop away after the very first outing. Begin by getting the owner's permission, since without it the work is unlawful and nothing that gets damaged is covered. Probe the soil next, because an old dump can hide broken glass or leaking drums, and a work party thrown together ends at the first-aid post. Hand out the jobs before the group shows up, because if people learn what to do only once they arrive, half the hands stand waiting at the gate. Bring thick gloves and more containers than seem necessary, since a heap left at the roadside pulls in further dumping. Close the day with food shared on the spot. Tiredness goes down better when it ends together, and the volunteers turn up again at the next outing.

units: an electrical failure leaves a residential sector without light
with the lifts stopped, elderly occupants are shut in at home
those occupants are left with no heat and no way to call
the failure itself is put right quickly
the real obstacle was that nobody knew which occupants were on their own
an employee of the library thinks up a cheap answer
a voluntary register of vulnerable homes is drawn up with the caretaker
two neighbors per floor are named to check the apartments when an alert comes
two later incidents passed off without panic
text: A failure on the network dropped the upper quarter into darkness, and the news climbed the stairwells landing by landing. With the elevators stopped, older residents stayed shut in their apartments, no heat, no charged phone. The hard part was never the outage, which was put right soon enough, but the blankness: nobody knew who lived alone behind which door. A woman who works at the library came forward with an answer that cost little and has lasted. Together with the caretaker she drew up a voluntary list of the homes where someone might have to be helped, then gave every floor a pair of neighbors charged with knocking when the next alert came. The list sleeps in a sealed envelope. Two alerts have passed since, neither with any panic, and the street claims to feel less anonymous.

units: two staircases in the same block share nothing but their height
one is built on a concrete frame
its wide straight steps throw sound back
its landings open onto corridors lit by a band of glass
the other, more worn, turns around a stone core
its steps are hollowed by use and its metal rail shifts
its light comes from a glazed opening at the top
the newer staircase carries noise from one end of the building to the other
the older one swallows sound but holds the damp
being narrow, the second forces the people using it to meet
text: Two staircases stand facing each other inside the same residential block, and nothing makes them comparable but their height. The one in the east wing rests on a concrete frame. Its steps are straight, wide and loud, and every landing opens onto a corridor lit by a band of glass. The one in the west wing is older and winds around a stone core. Its steps are hollowed in the middle from use, the wrought-iron rail shifts under the hand, and the light falls from a glazed opening right at the top. The first carries noise so effectively that a slammed door below resounds upstairs. The second swallows it, but it holds the damp, which means painting the walls over and over again. The people living in the old wing see more of each other, because the narrow turns oblige them to slow down.

units: protecting common life means naming what makes it fragile
the loss of ground open to free use is the first threat
what is left are places meant for buying
that shift cuts down the meetings between people unlike one another
a body that debates without ever concluding cheapens public speech
walling the generations apart separates childhood from old age
alarming stories turn the neighbor into a danger
the writer holds that this decay can be undone
modest acts such as backing a beginner mend the social bond
text: Defending our common life means naming, without flinching, everything that makes it fragile. First, the loss of ground open to everyone: once the benches go, what is left are places meant for buying, and we stop rubbing shoulders with anyone unlike ourselves. Then the heaviness of decision, because a body that debates and never concludes teaches its own members that public speech weighs nothing. Add the walling apart of the generations, which files each of us in a separate pen, childhood here, old age elsewhere. Add fear too, kept alive by stories that make the neighbor a danger before they make him a support. None of this, however, is settled for good. A society mends through ordinary acts: opening a room, backing a beginner, agreeing to lose an evening listening to a disagreement.
